comments.body:
> **Noor** · cohort peer · works in a regulated bank

Reviewing this from the regulated side, because I have shipped something close to it and the design has one assumption that will not survive contact.

**"ACL denormalised onto chunk + its own CDC stream."** With ~400 scopes expressed as line-of-business × jurisdiction × seniority, you are not storing 400 values — you are storing a *set* per chunk, and sets do not denormalise cleanly.

The failure is not on the read path, it is on the **re-grant**. Someone moves team, a jurisdiction's rules change, a whole LOB gets reorganised — and now you are rewriting the ACL field on some large fraction of 40M chunks. Your CDC stream is sized for document edits, which are rare. Permission changes are not rare and they are *bursty*: a reorganisation touches millions of chunks in one transaction.

What I would want to see argued: why not keep ACLs **out** of the chunk and evaluate a predicate at query time against a separate, small, fast-changing store? You pay a join; you stop paying a rewrite.

replies.body:
> **the original poster** · cohort

This is the strongest objection and I did not have a good answer to it at the time.

Where I would still defend denormalisation: **pre-filtering has to happen inside the retrieval query**, not after it. If ACLs live elsewhere, either you post-filter — which collapses `k` unpredictably and is the `k_collapse` failure notebook 03 measures — or you push a potentially enormous ID list into the query, which OpenSearch will not thank you for.

Where you are right and I would change the design: the ACL should be a **small denormalised group key**, not the full set. Chunks carry `acl_group_id`; the mapping from user to permitted group IDs is resolved at query time from the small fast store. A reorganisation then rewrites the *mapping*, not 40M chunks.

That is a materially better design and it came out of this comment.

> **Noor** · cohort peer · works in a regulated bank

Yes — that is the shape. One addition: version the group mapping and put the version in the trace. When someone asks in six months "could this user have seen this document on the 3rd of March", you need the mapping as it was, not as it is. Audit will ask. Ours did.

comments.body:
> **Marcus** · cohort peer

On cost — the design has "self-hosted encoder, GPU backfill budgeted separately". Separately from what? That reads like the line item that eats the project. If the corpus is 40M chunks and you re-embed on every encoder change, is that not the dominant cost in the whole system?

replies.body:
> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

It is usually the second-largest line and the most under-forecast, so pushing on it is right. But "budgeted separately" is defensible if it means *amortised differently*, which I read as the intent.

The distinction that matters: backfill is **capex-shaped** — large, infrequent, plannable. Serving is **opex-shaped** — smaller, continuous, scales with traffic. Blending them into one per-query number hides the fact that one of them is a decision you make twice a year and the other is a bill you pay every day.

Where I would push instead: **what is the re-embed trigger policy?** "Encoder change" is not a policy, it is an event. Without a written rule — how much quality gain justifies a week of GPU and a shadow evaluation — you get one of two failure modes: never upgrading, or upgrading on every release because someone read a benchmark. The design should name the threshold.

comments.body:
> **Dana** · reviewer · owns the eval harness

One thing missing from the design that will be the first question in an actual client review: **there is no evaluation plan.**

The diagram goes from documents to a handler. Nowhere does it say how you know it works, or how you would know it had stopped working. In a regulated context that is not a nice-to-have — "the model got worse and we noticed in week six" is a reportable event for some of these clients.

Concretely I would want, before any of the retrieval design:

- **Who writes the gold set, and when.** Twelve weeks with one of their engineers means the eval set competes with the build for the same person. Say which wins.
- **The frozen slice, agreed with them up front**, so that "better" has a definition neither side can move afterwards.
- **What blocks a release.** Your CI gate is the model for this and it belongs in the proposal, not in the implementation.
- **The abstention target.** In insurance, a confident wrong answer to a handler on a call is materially worse than a refusal, and that asymmetry should be a number before you build, not a discovery after.

Marking Dana's comment as the answer, because the missing evaluation plan is the defect that would actually lose this engagement, and the other two are refinements to a design that would otherwise be built without a definition of "working".

**Synthesis of the three critiques, and what changes:**

| Critique | Verdict | Change |
|---|---|---|
| ACL denormalisation does not survive re-grants (Noor) | **Accepted** | Chunks carry `acl_group_id`; user→groups resolved at query time; mapping is versioned and lands in the trace |
| Encoder backfill is under-forecast (Marcus/Rafael) | **Partly** | Capex/opex split stands. Missing piece is a written re-embed trigger policy with a quality threshold |
| No evaluation plan (Dana) | **Accepted** | Weeks 1–2 are the eval set and the frozen slice, agreed in writing, before any retrieval work |

**What stays as designed and why:** OpenSearch in-VPC, clause-level structural chunking, and hybrid-with-rerank all survive review unchanged. The residency constraint makes the first non-negotiable, and the other two are corpus-shaped decisions that this review did not challenge.

**What is still open**, and should be argued in its own thread rather than buried here: whether the inline guardrail is a model call or a classifier. That is [#35](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/discussions/35), and it is the same question with a different failure cost.
